> Please make sure you're running fair benchmarks (e.g. by alternating running one or the other first, and making sure they produce consistent results over several runs).

All of the runs I did were compiled on the same conditions and alternated. Updated the description.

I will be considering this PR as a requirement for #112039 (which also involves `AHashMap`) as some recently introduced bottleneck made that one slower.

Decided to benchmark all four situations over the current `master` (production release template, modified Bunnymark, 500 bunnies, 4 alternated runs, average FPS of 30 seconds):

| Run | `master` | PR | #112039 | PR + #112039 |
|-|-|-|-|-|
| 1 | 2378 | 2448 | 2352 | 2422 |
| 2 | 2435 | 2362 | 2265 | 2504 |
| 3 | 2400 | 2334 | 2398 | 2515 |
| 4 | 2357 | 2490 | 2345 | 2515 |
| **Average** | **2392** | **2408** | **2340** | **2489** |

A test without using GDScript is already in the main description.

I also need to mention that I got a better performance by force-inlining the `find`s again (got a 3.8% increase with it). Is force-inlining really a problem considering `HashMap` does it since it was first implemented and isn't even that larger?

I'm a bit concerned with the measurement numbers in this PR (and other recent ones). If we take the mean improvement, it amounts to 0.6% improvement. Which may well be a real improvement, but since it's lower than the deviation between individual runs, it's really hard to say for certain. Coupled with the fact that some of your recent PRs have had highly fluctuating measurements in between runs, and across different PRs cherry-picked together, I'm a bit sceptical that we're seeing real improvements here.

Please keep in mind that we should aim to address bottlenecks with PRs that have real-world impact, as described in our [optimization guidelines](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/optimization.html). 
To make a case-relevant example, I would expect `AHashMap` optimizations to have double-digit percentage performance improvements. I'm not sure this is still possible in `AHashMap`, since it's already pretty well optimized, but I'm not one to say no to numbers. 

So, while I'm still looking to benchmark this change myself, it's rather low priority for me since I think we have some much more worrisome and easy to address performance gaps in our implementations. Some can be hard to find or fix, but when we do, they usually show much more convincing numbers on measurement.

> If we take the mean improvement, it amounts to 0.6% improvement.

If we take the sole `AHashMap` test alone, it would amount to at least 2.96% (lowest before compared to highest after, to take the worst case scenario). Remember that a GDScript test has more overhead than just `AHashMap` lookups and is more prone to fluctuations.

Note that in many cases, replacing `HashMap` with `AHashMap` may either cause mixed results or a slowdown, something I've seen many times and is now visible in #112039. And on the latter, having this PR on top actually sped things up even placing that on top of this.

> Coupled with the fact that some of your recent PRs have had highly fluctuating measurements in between runs, and across different PRs cherry-picked together, I'm a bit sceptical that we're seeing real improvements here.

So, is this PR being judged more by my previous PRs than by itself?

Rewrote the description to add a few details on what was changed and why.

The loop benchmark was placed on top as I believe that one has more relevance to this, and I also included a benchmark on empty map to cover the `unlikely()` change.

If we inline `find()` (something ivor was against, but I didn't find any regressions in the cases I tested) and make its `meta_idx` `static` (which should be safe as the variable only exists to make `_lookup_idx()` work, then gets completely discarded) we get interesting results:

#### Filled map

| Run | `master` | PR + inlined `find()` + static `meta_idx` in `find()` |
|-|-|-|
| 1 | 5.08 | 4.71 |
| 2 | 5.10 | 4.71 |
| 3 | 5.10 | 4.68 |
| 4 | 5.09 | 4.70 |
| 5 | 5.09 | 4.71 |

Minimum increase of **7.28%**

#### Empty map

| Run | `master` | PR + inlined `find()` + static `meta_idx` in `find()` |
|-|-|-|
| 1 | 0.331 | 0.247 |
| 2 | 0.336 | 0.242 |
| 3 | 0.330 | 0.247 |
| 4 | 0.344 | 0.244 |
| 5 | 0.330 | 0.242 |

Minimum increase of **25.15%**

Before anyone asks: I made sure to test both changes separately before making the claim.

@Ivorforce Is this a reasonable place to have double-digit percentage improvement? It will be a rare case, *unless* we start replacing certain `HashMap`s with `AHashMap`s.

Like I mentioned before, there are some cases where replacing `HashMap` with `AHashMap` would cause slowdowns instead of improving anything. I started all of this because I suspected `AHashMap` had some kind of bottleneck, and at least one slowdown got converted into an improvement.

Not sure if I'm playing with fire, but I threw in the changes mentioned above, and they didn't seem to break anything so far.

Updated benchmark results. All done in C++ with no Bunnymark involvement. One situation easily reached a **25.15%** improvement.

Please compare the build size with and without the forced inlining, both in dev and release builds, if the compiler thinks it's too big for inlining that's something to evaluate, and compare against the performance benefits 

Edit: I'd also be weary of any performance improvement from a simple inlining, it seems like it'd be due to the benchmarking setup rather than any real-world improvement, especially since `getptr` doesn't see comparable improvements in performance despite being essentially identical *and* that `find` needs to construct an iterator

Removing one level of call from this call chain, filled with far more complex operations, should have at most a negligible performance benefit I'd say, so I'd do some extra work to ensure that the benchmark actually measures what the method will do in real conditions, the compiler should be pretty good at optimizing the call through various means

Edit 2: Also might be completely off but the 0.333 seconds for 50 million lookups in an empty map seems fast, it's around 18 clock cycles at 2.7 GHz, assuming the chrono system time is global time for the machine (i.e. with task switching) that seems fast to me, and with the optimized case that's 13 cycles (12 with the new measurement). Maybe modern CPUs do a lot of extra work with those cycles but still, with the `getptr` it's just 9 cycles, which to me seems like it's just measuring the loop

Note that the L2 cache lookup for a processor of this era is on the same order of magnitude as the time per loop iteration of this benchmark

So outlined some of my concerns above about this looking like the benchmark measures *data* optimizations not behavioral optimizations, i.e. optimizing on *known* data and not general data

I might be off with my evaluation but it warrants a closer inspection

But still the time for the empty lookup is so marginal in absolute time with so many lookups that I don't think it'll actually matter in practice, the savings per cycle would be around 1-2 ns which would be negligible when compared to cache misses, in this case potentially at least two, one for the code and one for the data, even in relatively hot code I'd argue cache penalties would overshadow any savings, in the other cases the savings would be comparable at a few ns each

That is assuming the benchmarks measure real performance and doesn't benefit from known data 

Also is the benchmark code accurate? It shows either measuring just `getptr` or measuring *both* that'll give misleading results (possibly in both directions)

Also to clarify: this is not me disbelieving *you* or implying you've manipulated anything, I disbelieve the results being representative because of potential pitfalls in doing benchmarking

> Please compare the build size with and without the forced inlining, both in dev and release builds, if the compiler thinks it's too big for inlining that's something to evaluate, and compare against the performance benefits

Linux builds with `production=yes target=template_release`:

| Build | Size (bytes) |
|-|-|
| `master` | 68673464 |
| PR | 68677560 |
| PR (inline reverted) | 68677560 |
| PR (inline and more lookup funcs reverted)| 68677560 |

All situations of this PR had a 4 KiB increase. That in consideration, for this PR I believe inlining is much more desirable than not inlining.

Ironically, if we combine this with other AHashMap-related PRs like #112039 (which this PR turns from a bottleneck from an actual improvement), the size goes back down.

Please try with a dev build to see without LTO, the fact that the size is identical with and without inlining indicates that something optimizes it out somewhere, and that either the forced inline is reversed, or that it doesn't make any real difference in builds (that would indicate that the inlining having any performance impact might be a result of the benchmark conditions as well, so might be a hint that it won't matter in real conditions), it could just be that the inlining is negated by something else but it's suspicious that it doesn't affect the build size

It might be that it replaces a call with some tail optimization etc., meaning it can still have an effect on performance, but it is potentially indicative of something in the benchmark

Built with `dev_build=yes target=template_release`:

| Build | Size (bytes) |
|-|-|
| `master` | 734702440 |
| PR | 734885632 |
| PR (inline reverted) | 734885632 |

I should mention there are very few uses of `AHashMap::find()` in the engine, something that would increase a bit with #112039.

Honestly, I don't think build sizes are accurate to indicate whether the compiler is optimizing something or not. What if it does, but in the end the build size ends up the same?

Take my [QOA PR](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/91014) as an extreme example: Despite adding a lot of code and making more template functions, the build size actually *decreased*.

It is an indication that the inlining doesn't change in those builds, or that it is immaterial some other way, or the binary size would grow I'd say

But that indicates that the inline might be a red herring for optimization

Never said it indicated optimization or not, but obviously if the binary size remains the same the method wasn't inlined if that's the only difference in the build, and ergo the inlining cannot possibly affect performance in real code, which means that at minimum the effect of inlining in the benchmark doesn't affect the running code making the benchmark not representative of real code behavior

I wouldn't read too much into build size changes below 0.1% (~150kb). Compilers are black magic and one change can easily lead to many other changes that can unexpectedly increase or reduce the build size.
That being said, `_FORCE_INLINE_` is already overused, and should be avoided by default. There _are_ situations where it makes sense to use them (e.g. trivial getter functions), but functions with logic aren't one of those situations.

Don't forget that using `dev_build=yes` changes what `_FORCE_INLINE_` does. It's an `inline` in dev builds or size_extra builds but otherwise is an `_ALWAYS_INLINE_` (which defaults to `__attribute__((force_inline))` in my system and isn't precisely the same thing as `inline`)

I ran the filled find benchmark once again to compare with and without `_FORCE_INLINE_`:

### With `_FORCE_INLINE_`

| Run | `master` | PR |
|-|-|-|
| 1 | 5.07 | 4.57 |
| 2 | 5.07 | 4.57 |
| 3 | 5.07 | 4.55 |
| 4 | 5.06 | 4.55 |
| 5 | 5.09 | 4.56 |

### Without `_FORCE_INLINE_`

| Run | `master` | PR |
|-|-|-|
| 1 | 5.03 | 4.78 |
| 2 | 5.01 | 4.78 |
| 3 | 5.00 | 4.78 |
| 4 | 5.01 | 4.77 |
| 5 | 4.99 | 4.78 |

If `_FORCE_INLINE_` is "doing nothing" by comparing build sizes but benchmarks say otherwise, why can't we give the benefit of doubt and leave it in?

> That being said, `_FORCE_INLINE_` is already overused, and should be avoided by default. There are situations where it makes sense to use them (e.g. trivial getter functions), but functions with logic aren't one of those situations.

> If `_FORCE_INLINE_` is "doing nothing" by comparing build sizes but benchmarks say otherwise, why can't we give the benefit of doubt?

No that's an indication to *look closer* as it means it might be a red herring, we shouldn't add it if we can't prove it actually helps

The benchmark can be victim to any number of incorrect optimizations that don't reflect reality but are measurable, for example if the benchmark optimizes out a lot of the actual code because it knows the hash map is empty or knows what is in it, and the difference in performance is just reflecting the benefit of inlining when the rest of the method is effectively empty, I'd suggest trying with `_NO_INLINE_` and see if *that* affects the binary, if it does that just means that the method is inlined by default

I'd suggest analyzing the assembly of the benchmark code and seeing if it looks reasonable, and testing different benchmarks to eliminate special behavior under test being a problem

It doesn't have to be anything but if the inlining looks like it doesn't affect the compiled code yet has an effect on performance that's a red flag, without having run the code I can't say but I would suspect the compiler just optimizes out all the code when it knows the map is empty (that's what it *should* be doing if nothing is stopping it, and I can't see any reason the benchmark would prevent that)

And as Ivorforce says this function shouldn't have force inlining

> The benchmark can be victim to any number of incorrect optimizations that don't reflect reality but are measurable, for example if the benchmark optimizes out a lot of the actual code because it knows the hash map is empty or knows what is in it, and the difference in performance is just reflecting the benefit of inlining when the rest of the method is effectively empty

> It doesn't have to be anything but if the inlining looks like it doesn't affect the compiled code yet has an effect on performance that's a red flag, without having run the code I can't say but I would suspect the compiler just optimizes out all the code when it knows the map is empty

Right, but the benchmark I posted above covers the filled situation, not an empty map. The compiler is certainly not optimizing it for an empty map.

> That being said, `_FORCE_INLINE_` is already overused, and should be avoided by default. There are situations where it makes sense to use them (e.g. trivial getter functions), but functions with logic aren't one of those situations.

> And as Ivorforce says this function shouldn't have force inlining

Why does `HashMap::find()` do it then? And I doubt removing the force-inline from it would make sense from a performance point of view.

The empty case is the trivial to explain by compiler behavior, but it's possible in the filled case too, but a quick check with compiled output would dismiss the concern that it optimizes too much in the benchmark, any optimizer worth its salt should optimize out all the checks against `_elements` in the benchmark as it knows it's not null, or is null in the empty case (in fact the compiler might chose to just inline much more of the function tree as it's used exactly once)

The fact that `HashMap` has this is not relevant it might be wrong too but it shouldn't be added here on the assumption that because it has it this should too, so let's not reference it as a data point but ensure the benchmark is reasonable

But IMO the force inline having any effect on the performance, one that relatively large, is questionable in real world cases it essentially removes one call and perhaps one cache miss at first but in the general case it's negligible and might be worse because of other factors

But in summary: the forced inline should be confirmed as being relevant and the benchmarks should be checked so they don't accidentally optimize based on known data 

Edit: the first step should be to ensure the benchmarks are reliable, before doing any more changing or decision, so we know that changes to the PR actually are proven performance benefits

As much as I wanted to not resort to Bunnymark, it was the only place I could test `AHashMap::find()` in a way it would take a significant amount of CPU cycles. It was just a matter of pushing a bit further so the FPS wouldn't oscillate that much.

By testing this PR combined with #112039 with and without inlining `find()`, I measured that not inlining made it about 2.5% faster.

Will revert the `_FORCE_INLINE_`s yet again and redo the benchmarks.

Please try compiling and analyzing the assembly, to make sure the results are actually useful, it knowing that the container is empty or not likely excludes code, it also might remove parts of the code that isn't used which affects the cache behavior 

With some of these benchmarks differing in merely nanoseconds it is critical to evaluate exactly what is going on, if it is a real optimization or not, and if the optimization matters in real cases and if it doesn't cause regressions in performance instead through code duplication for example

Benchmarks redone.

Turns out the compiler was in fact optimizing for an empty map. I added some code to attempt to bypass it (add one element, then reset) and seems it worked on the `find()` case, making the result go sub 1%. On the other hand, the `getptr()` case didn't seem affected.

That's great progress! I'd still evaluate the compiled results and ensure there aren't some other test specific issues with the benchmarks

The code duplication risks being less of a measurable issue in a benchmark for example, so would be good to ensure the test context is complete and doesn't exclude code, and probably to run multiple benchmarks in the same run of the code so it doesn't optimize differently, the code duplication being a serious risk both for general performance and maintenance burden

Test code and benchmarks updated. This time all the runs are in one file, which should make the results much more accurate but maybe not 100% trustworthy. At least the `getptr()` case seems to have been affected now.

The new benchmarks look more effective and the results look much more reasonable I'd say.

But as we refine the benchmarks the gains shrink drastically which indicates to me that we'd need to continue refining them to make sure the gains don't continue to shrink, and we also have significant gains in only one area, which might be a fluke itself would warrant more investigation.

We've done a lot of back and forth on this so won't ask you to do more work now and we'll let the core team give some feedback on this, but I would like to add the following final notes of mine for now:
* This would need benchmarking on all behaviors to make sure we don't have regressions in other areas, the mutating methods both insertion and erasure for example
* The benchmarks just by their absolute values show that the type is very, *very* well optimized already, so we should be careful to not hunt the last margins and risk regressions
* The benchmarks are not necessarily representative of real use, especially as already mentioned the cache is very hot in these tests, I'd also suggest running with different distributions of data as the current tests for full maps have all the keys be present which might give false results, and we'd risk regressions on the worst cases
* On that note of hot caches, in even the best result we have about 10 ns per iteration (best case, assuming the benchmark ran with 100% CPU utilization on its core and thread, which I can't say how likely it is), which I feel is not necessarily gonna matter in real use with cold cache, especially if the splitting of the methods causes more of the code to be split into different cache lines, worst case I'd say a single lookup with cold cache would cause at least 2 and probably 3 or 4 cache misses (one or two instruction and one or two data, depending on the layout), that could easily erase all the gains on its own
* As already mentioned the method that has the greatest gains is also the one that has the least uses (if any, not sure if the const find method has any uses), and even for the other cases the methods are extremely rarely used, so I'm not sure there's any real likelihood that this will have any real benefits
* Finally the splitting of the methods has costs, both in code complexity (causing harder to maintain code by duplication, risking errors when failing to duplicate changes) and in risk of performance regressions due to cache fitting, the latter can be tricky as it depends on a lot of factors and even specific hardware, and even the marginal increase in binary size is a cost to consider given the otherwise very small gains

In summary I don't think this PR is worth the costs for such, in absolute terms, marginal gains, especially with the above considerations

Closing. This was an attempt of mine to blindly solve a (maybe not real) problem by doing a massive refactor.

In any case, I'd say this is superseded by #121439, which calls attention to an actual design issue within `AHashMap` and diff is tiny.
